questions.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 6 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form using the standard algorithm for Gaussian elimination, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 6 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-1\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 5 & 6 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 16 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{16}\cdot {R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{13}{16}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 2x-4y=6 \\  & 4x-7y=10.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 6 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 6 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x-2y=3 \\  & y=-2,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-2$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(-2)=3\,⇒\,x=-1.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-1$ and $y=-2.$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/baf05a693deacc3ef644165bae4de7b1435a90c73f050ac76c48892b2e010393.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=1$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+2(1)=0 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-2$ and $y=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\left<  -2,1 \right>.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations and its respective **augmented matrix**:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/2c5dfe046037750f98f773ad906094f5ffbad3c285adf200134a119f72888ac8.svg)

If we can convert the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form, then we can solve the system using back substitution.

The procedure for reducing $M$ to row echelon form using elementary row operations is called **Gaussian elimination**. To perform Gaussian elimination on a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we use the following procedure.

**Step 1:** Consider the entry $a_{11}=2$ of the coefficient matrix. This entry is called a **pivot element**. We want to make this entry equal to $1$. So, the first elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_1 := \dfrac{1}{2}R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Consider the entry $a_{21}=3$ below the first pivot element. We want to make this entry equal to $0$. So, the second elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=R_2+(-3)R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, consider the entry $a_{22}=-10$. This entry is the second pivot element, and we would like to make it equal to $1$. So, the third elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=\dfrac{1}{-10}R_2
$$

and we get $M$ in row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{-10}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/b83c4646349bada803311e5e9e160aafc8f08e6f51c7b69302def5ca4eeaa3fa.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+3 \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = -1 
	\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
	x=\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Or, in vector form, $\left< \dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right>.$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, consider the entry $a_{22}=-10$. This entry is the second pivot element, and we would like to make it equal to $1$. So, the third elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=\dfrac{1}{-10}R_2
$$

and we get $M$ in row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{-10}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/b83c4646349bada803311e5e9e160aafc8f08e6f51c7b69302def5ca4eeaa3fa.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+3 \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = -1 
	\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
	x=\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Or, in vector form, $\left< \dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right>.$

tutorials.name: The Uniqueness of the Row Echelon Form Matrix
tutorials.problem:
The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique. In the previous example, after the first row operation we arrived at 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/ebcb9bc5aedf609284436ad1c10e98f9b22d91a382136b5aabfb3f18c736ddae.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/536245bdc7fc9dab02723d3576adff774dfd9711551f472333c027d83f76c05b.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

tutorials.content:
The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique. In the previous example, after the first row operation we arrived at

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118684/assets/536245bdc7fc9dab02723d3576adff774dfd9711551f472333c027d83f76c05b.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

lesson_definition.title: Solving 2x2 Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

steps.title: Introduction
steps.html:
Introduction
?

Consider the following system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:

If we can convert the augmented matrix to row echelon form, then we can solve the system using back substitution.

The procedure for reducing to row echelon form using elementary row operations is called Gaussian elimination. To perform Gaussian elimination on a matrix, we use the following procedure.
